## My Reasoning

I've been farming in Quzhou my whole life. The land here tells you what to grow — it's the North China Plain, so it's winter wheat and summer maize, same as my father did, same as my neighbors do. The market infrastructure is built around these two crops, the equipment cooperatives service them, and I know them deeply. At 65, I'm not going to experiment with something unfamiliar.

Water is what keeps me up at night. The water table here has dropped every decade I've been farming. My county has pushed the spray irrigation program, but I haven't converted my fields — I'll manage by being disciplined: three irrigations for wheat instead of four, less topdressing water for the maize. My education helps me here. I've read enough from the county agricultural bureau to know where yield response to water starts to flatten.

For wheat, I'll use Jimai 22 — a proven semi-dwarf variety that performs well on my soil type. For corn, Zhengdan 958 again. I know its growth curve. I've seen younger farmers chase newer hybrids and get burned in a bad year. I won't do that.

After the wheat is cut in June, I'll direct-sow the corn into the stubble. No-tillage saves me fuel and time, and at 65 with my son only available on weekends, that matters. For the wheat planting in October, I'll run the rotary tiller — the soil needs that refresh after summer corn.

I'm keeping 3 mu near the house in garlic. It's labor-intensive at harvest, but my wife helps, and the local traders pay well for Quzhou garlic. It also breaks the disease cycle compared to pure wheat-corn.

I'll apply fertilizer based on what I know about my plots — they're moderately fertile from decades of organic returns. I won't over-apply nitrogen the way the younger men do. Phosphorus and potassium I'll split between base dressing and a light top-up.
